Legal framework for Internet Shutdown in India

Context: During the "Chalo Sansad" protest organised by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), Mobile Internet Service were shut down in parts of Central Delhi.

Provisions:

~Under Section 20(2)(b) of the Telecommunication Act, 2023 and the Telecommunications (Temporary Suspension of Services) Rules, 2024, Telecommunication services may be suspended.

~Suspension can be ordered only on the occurrence of a public emergency or in the interest of public safety on the grounds specified in that provision, and for reasons recorded in writing.

~Orders must be reasoned, published, geographically and temporarily limited and consider whether less restrictive measures are sufficient.

Under the 2024 Rules, a suspension order cannot remain in force for more than 15 days.

Supreme Court Guidelines:

~In Anuradha Bhasin v Union of India (2020), the Supreme Court linked Internet access with freedoms under Articles 19(1) (a) and 19(1)(g).

~Shutdowns must satisfy necessity and proportionality, be the least restrictive measures, and remain open to judicial review.

Suspension can be challenged in court?
Yes. Under Article 226 before a High Court and Article 32 before the Supreme Court.

India's Position:
India recorded about 24 Internet shutdowns in 2026 till July 22; Jammu & Kashmir has recorded the highest cumulative number since 2012.

Pic created by AI

Statement : IFF condemns the internet shutdown in parts of Central Delhi. No suspension order has been made public.

New Delhi, 20 July 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) condemns the suspension of mobile internet services imposed today, 20 July 2026, in parts of Central Delhi, including the area around Jantar Mantar. The shutdown coincided with the 'Chalo Sansad' march called by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) on the opening day of the Monsoon Session of Parliament, where thousands of students and young people had gathered to press their demands. Permission for the march was refused. Prohibitory orders were imposed under Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023. Routes to Parliament were sealed, and metro stations including, Patel Chowk, Rajiv Chowk and Janpath were closed. Amid reports of the use of force to disperse protesters, mobile internet was then switched off, reportedly "as a precautionary measure". We urge the immediate restoration of all telecommunication services in the capital and an end to internet shutdowns across India.

The developments of today are of immense consequence to the future of our democracy. The voices gathered at Jantar Mantar, and the residents of the national capital, need to be heard the loudest, not silenced en masse.

No order has been made public

At the time of release of this statement, no copy of any suspension order has been published by the Ministry of Home Affairs, the Department of Telecommunications, the Government of NCT of Delhi or the Delhi Police. Residents of the capital do not know which authority directed the shutdown, on what grounds, over which precise areas, for which services, or for what duration. An unpublished order is an unaccountable order. It cannot be challenged before a court, and the judicial review guaranteed by the Supreme Court becomes illusory. Some reports further indicate the deployment of network jammers in parts of Central Delhi, including near Jantar Mantar. Jamming equipment finds no sanction in the legal framework for the suspension of telecommunication services at all. If jammers were deployed, the government must disclose under what legal authority.

Binding safeguards violated

On 10 January 2020, the Supreme Court in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India, (2020) 3 SCC 637 held that the freedom of speech and expression, and the freedom to carry on trade or business through the medium of the internet, are protected under Articles 19(1)(a) and 19(1)(g) of the Constitution. The Court directed that every order suspending telecom services must be published. Reasons must be recorded in writing. The restriction must be proportionate, adopting the least restrictive measure available. It cannot continue indefinitely. It is subject to judicial review, and to scrutiny by a review committee.

Parliament has since replaced the framework of the Indian Telegraph Act, 1885. Under Section 20(2)(b) of the Telecommunications Act, 2023, telecommunication services may be suspended only on the occurrence of a public emergency or in the interest of public safety, on the grounds specified in that provision, and for reasons recorded in writing. The Telecommunications (Temporary Suspension of Services) Rules, 2024, notified on 22 November 2024, give effect to this power. A suspension order may be issued only by the Union Home Secretary or the State Home Secretary. An officer not below the rank of Joint Secretary may act in unavoidable circumstances, subject to confirmation by the competent authority within twenty four hours. Every order must clearly define the geographical area and the specific services suspended, and cannot remain in operation beyond fifteen days. Every order must also be published. A Review Committee must meet within five days of the order and record its findings on whether it complies with Section 20(2).

These safeguards are not being followed

If we account for today's shutdown against this legal architecture. The order is unpublished, in breach of Anuradha Bhasin and the Suspension Rules, 2024 alike. No recorded reasons are available to the public despite little to no reports of violence and consistent calls for the protest to be peaceful by the CJP and other organisers. The precise areas and services covered are undisclosed and so is the duration. Whether the competent authority even issued the order cannot be known. Whether the Review Committee will examine it cannot be verified. While the Suspension Rules prescribe no outer time limit for publication, a gap we have previously flagged, it cannot cut against the spirit of the Anuradha Bhasin judgement. A blanket suspension across densely populated parts of the capital, imposed as a "precaution" against a march to Parliament, is the opposite of a narrowly tailored, least restrictive measure. A shutdown timed to a protest restricts the freedoms of speech and assembly at the very moment they matter most.

The human cost of a shutdown

Access to the internet is a digital right on which the exercise of our fundamental freedoms now depends. When the network goes dark in Central Delhi, a journalist at Jantar Mantar cannot file her report or broadcast live. A street vendor on the surrounding roads cannot accept a UPI payment. A gig worker loses a day's earnings. A parent cannot confirm that a child who joined the march is safe. Cutting off communications prevents people from reaching out for help and manufactures panic in a moment which demands calm. These costs fall hardest on daily wage earners and small traders who can least absorb them. Internet based communications also promote trust between people and their government. 

A pattern, not an aberration

Delhi has seen this before. On 19 December 2019, mobile services were suspended for the first time in the capital's history during the protests against the Citizenship (Amendment) Act, in areas including Seelampur, Jamia Nagar and Mandi House. On 26 January 2021, the Ministry of Home Affairs suspended internet services in Singhu, Ghazipur, Tikri, Mukarba Chowk, Nangloi and their adjoining areas during the farmers' protests. According to the #KeepItOn coalition's report released in March 2026, India recorded 65 internet shutdowns in 2025, the highest of any democracy in the world, and accounts for 920 of the 2,102 shutdowns documented globally since 2016. We have consistently advocated against the harm these disruptions cause, from Jammu and Kashmir to Rajasthan, and from Haryana to Manipur, where a shutdown in 2023 ran for over two hundred days. The orders are rarely published on time, and the findings of review committees never see daylight.

Our demands

We call upon the Government of India and the Government of NCT of Delhi to:

1. Immediately restore all suspended telecommunication and internet services in Central Delhi.
2. Publish forthwith every suspension order passed on or around 20 July 2026, together with the reasons recorded in writing, as mandated by Anuradha Bhasin and the Telecommunications (Temporary Suspension of Services) Rules, 2024.
3. Disclose the issuing authority, the grounds, the precise areas and services covered, and the period of operation, and clarify whether network jammers were deployed and under what legal authority.
4. Place the order before the Review Committee within five days as required by the Rules, and make its findings public.
5. Reform Section 20(2)(b) of the Telecommunications Act, 2023 to provide for independent prior authorisation and real consequences for unlawful suspensions.

IFF will file applications under the Right to Information Act, 2005 seeking copies of the suspension orders and the records of the Review Committee, and is examining further legal remedies. 

Delhi and all of India deserve better.

Senior Researcher Dr. Sanjana Hattotuwa has raised questions over the continued visibility of betting-linked surrogate brands during Sri Lanka Cricket matches, despite regulatory action against unlicensed online gambling platforms in the country.

In an analysis of highlights from the second Test between Sri Lanka and India at the SSC, Hattotuwa said the 1xBAT logo received around 14 minutes of screen exposure across five daily highlights packages published by Sri Lanka Cricket.

The five videos had collectively recorded more than 629,000 views at the time of his analysis. Combined with highlights from the first Test in Galle, Hattotuwa estimated that 1xBAT received around 25 minutes of exposure across 10 videos viewed around two million times.

He said 1xBAT branding appeared through an advertising mat behind the wicket, boundary advertising and sight-screen placements during the SSC Test. Sri Lanka Cricket’s website confirms that official highlights from the Test were published on its channels.

Hattotuwa also highlighted the presence of Parimatch Sports and batbricks7 during the second Test, describing them as surrogate brands linked to offshore betting operations.

The researcher questioned how such advertising could continue while Sri Lankan authorities were taking action against unlicensed online gambling websites.

The Telecommunications Regulatory Commission of Sri Lanka had earlier moved to block access to several gambling websites, including https://t.co/hbVX8m2cGa. Hattotuwa argues that 1xBAT functions as a surrogate brand for 1xBet, an association that has previously been acknowledged by a former Sri Lanka Cricket secretary.

The Gambling Regulatory Authority Act No. 17 of 2025 includes provisions governing the operation and promotion of unlicensed online gambling.

Sri Lanka Cricket, however, has previously said it “does not permit betting advertising at SLC matches within the territory of Sri Lanka.”

From antitrust actions reshaping India's digital gaming landscape to cybercrime crackdowns and smartphone-driven gaming growth, today's press review captures the forces defining the gambling and lotteries sector. 1. CCI Closes Google Real Money Games Probe
A front-page report in Free Press Journal says the Competition Commission has officially closed its case against Google over real money games, pointing to the recent enforcement of the Online Gaming Act as an exceptional development. The legal battle began in two thousand twenty-two when Winzo Games accused the tech giant of unfairly restricting gambling applications and advertisements on its application store. After the regulator launched a detailed investigation in two thousand twenty-four, Google agreed to modify its practices before the new gaming framework took full effect.
Why it matters: The Competition Commission's closure of its Google case marks a pivotal shift in how real money games are regulated in India.
Key detail: The case, filed by Winzo Games in 2022, was investigated under the Online Gaming Act, with Google committing to modify its practices before the new framework took full effect.
Source: Free Press Journal, Mumbai, 9 September 2026
Next step: Stakeholders should monitor how the Online Gaming Act reshapes app store policies and advertising norms across India's digital gaming ecosystem.

2. Slice, Unacademy: Unicorn Valuations Reset
A front-page report in Times of India says unicorn valuations across gaming, edtech, and fintech sectors have sharply corrected following a recent real-money gaming ban and a broader reset in private market expectations. Unacademy was acquired by rival upGrad in an all-stock deal valued at just over two hundred million dollars, a significant drop from its peak valuation of three point four billion dollars in two thousand twenty-one, while Slice investors now assess the firm as a banking company rather than a fintech. Investors are placing greater weight on fundamentals, growth efficiency, and profitability after seeing pushback from public markets, with many companies that raised capital on vanity metrics struggling to justify previous rounds.
Why it matters: The sharp correction in unicorn valuations across gaming, edtech, and fintech reflects a fundamental reset in how private markets value growth.
Key detail: Unacademy was acquired by upGrad in an all-stock deal valued at just over $200 million, down from a peak of $3.4 billion in 2021; Slice investors now classify it as a banking company.
Source: Times of India, New Delhi
Next step: Founders and CFOs should reassess growth strategies around fundamentals, profitability, and sustainable metrics rather than vanity valuations.

3. Hyderabad Police Crack Down on Cybercrime
A front-page report in Deccan Chronicle says that Hyderabad city cybercrime police arrested 47 suspects across seven states last month, registering 65 cases through the National Cybercrime Reporting Portal. Authorities recovered digital devices and refunded approximately ninety nine lakhs of rupees to victims while dismantling hundreds of fraudulent social media profiles and advertisements linked to investment scams, illegal betting, and child exploitation. Additional Commissioner M. Srinivasulu highlighted ongoing patrols and victim guidance initiatives aimed at curbing identity theft and online fraud across the country.
Why it matters: The arrest of 47 suspects across seven states highlights the growing sophistication of cybercrime networks targeting Indian users.
Key detail: Police registered 65 cases through the National Cybercrime Reporting Portal, recovered digital devices, refunded approximately 99 lakhs of rupees, and dismantled hundreds of fraudulent profiles linked to investment scams, illegal betting, and child exploitation.
Source: Deccan Chronicle, Hyderabad, 8 September 2026
Next step: Organizations should strengthen digital forensics capabilities and victim support systems as cyber threats evolve.

4. Sandoz Targets Biosimilars Growth
A front-page report in Economic Times says Swiss drugmaker Sandoz aims to more than double its annual net sales by 2035, with a majority coming from biosimilar medicines. The company plans to increase its biosimilars portfolio to 100 drugs by 2040 from 13 currently, targeting mid-to-high single-digit percentage growth in total annual net sales at constant currencies from 2025 to 2030. Separately, the Competition Commission of India closed a case against Google over real-money games citing exceptional developments, including the implementation of the Online Gaming Act.
Why it matters: Sandoz's ambitious expansion into biosimilars signals a broader pharmaceutical transformation that intersects with regulatory and competition dynamics.
Key detail: The Swiss drugmaker aims to more than double annual net sales by 2035, growing its biosimilars portfolio from 13 to 100 drugs by 2040.
Source: Economic Times, London
Next step: Investors and pharma executives should track how biosimilar pipelines align with India's evolving healthcare and competition frameworks.

5. Smartphones Boost Gaming Uptake
A front-page report in Economic Times says smartphones are driving gaming uptake worldwide. A survey of one thousand to eight thousand six hundred respondents aged eighteen to sixty-four across South Africa, Zambia, the United States, China, and Colombia from July two thousand twenty-five to June two thousand twenty-six found varying shares of frequent and occasional gamers.

text:
One Year Later, Charlie Kirk’s Faith Is Still Bearing Fruit

Three weeks before Charlie Kirk was killed, a reporter sat down with him expecting to talk about politics. That would have been the obvious conversation. Charlie had spent his adult life building Turning Point USA, debating students on college campuses, influencing elections, and becoming one of the most recognizable conservative voices in America. Yet during that August 19, 2025 interview with the Deseret News, Charlie kept returning to something deeper. “I could talk about religion all day long,” he told the reporter.

A year after his death, I think that conversation tells us more about Charlie Kirk than another accounting of elections, endorsements, or viral debates ever could. His Christian faith was not something he discovered near the end of his life, and it would be dishonest to portray his final months as a conversion from politics to Christianity. Faith had been woven through his public work for years. What was becoming clearer was the order of things. Charlie increasingly understood that changing a person's political opinions meant very little if the person himself remained unchanged.

The habits he described shortly before his death give us a window into that development. Charlie read Scripture every day. At night he spent time examining his conscience. He observed a phone free Sabbath from Friday evening until Saturday sunset, deliberately removing himself from the endless argument that had become part of his daily life. He was planning a book about setting aside one day in seven to honor God. These were not memories polished after his death by grieving friends. Charlie described them himself while he was still alive, long before anyone knew those words would become part of his final testimony.

Even more revealing was the future he wanted for the young people who listened to him. He wanted to point them toward what he called “ultimate purposes.” He spoke about returning to church and faith, getting married, having children, and pursuing virtue rather than remaining trapped in anger. He understood that success might actually mean young people spending less time online consuming political content, including his own. For a man who had built one of the most successful conservative media operations in the country, that admission deserves attention.

Most people who make their living online need you to keep watching. Charlie was beginning to describe success as helping people build lives in which they needed to watch him less.

That is where I think the deeper change was occurring. Charlie never stopped believing that ideas had consequences or that Christians had responsibilities in public life. He did not abandon politics as his faith deepened. His faith increasingly gave his politics their place and their limits. He could spend an afternoon debating public policy and still understand that winning an argument could not make someone righteous, repair a marriage, raise a child, conquer sin, or reconcile a person to God.

His political convictions and Christian convictions were therefore not as easily separated as some descriptions of his life suggest. On questions such as abortion, marriage, sexuality, family, the responsibilities of men and women, and the moral order of society, Charlie believed his positions followed from truths larger than a party platform. They were political because those questions had entered politics, but he understood them first as moral questions shaped by his reading of Scripture.

That does not mean every political judgment Charlie ever made should be granted biblical authority. No Christian politician, activist, writer, or voter gets that privilege. Scripture does not provide a party platform, and Christians can reach different prudential conclusions while remaining faithful to the same Lord. But neither should we pretend that Charlie merely attached Christianity to a set of political preferences he had formed somewhere else. On many of the issues for which he became most controversial, he believed he was defending a Christian understanding of human beings, marriage, family, sex, responsibility, and truth.

That distinction becomes especially important when we consider the hostility he faced.

Charlie knew people wanted him dead. In May 2025, during a faith based gathering in Phoenix, he spoke openly about death threats against himself and his family. He had security because of the politicians and values he supported, and he had discussed receiving threats on other occasions as well. This was not an abstract possibility that became visible only after September 10. He knew the danger existed and continued showing up.

There had also been public events where opposition to his appearances crossed into violence. At a 2023 event at the University of California, Davis, protesters broke ten glass panes at the venue and threw eggs and other objects, and an officer was injured after being pushed to the ground. Charlie himself was not physically attacked in that incident. The episode shows only what the evidence permits us to say: disagreement surrounding some of his appearances had already become capable of producing property damage and injury.

Charlie continued showing up.

A year after his murder, the alleged motive makes the relationship between his faith and his public witness even harder to dismiss. Prosecutors allege that Tyler Robinson targeted Charlie because of his political and religious beliefs. Their case has specifically pointed to Charlie's views concerning homosexuality, same sex marriage, and gender transition. Robinson's defense disputes whether prosecutors have established that motive, and the criminal case has not reached a final judgment. That distinction has to remain clear. But the prosecution's theory is significant because the very beliefs it identifies as possible reasons Charlie was targeted were beliefs Charlie publicly connected to Christian morality.

For that reason, I am no longer comfortable treating the question of martyrdom as something Christians should simply dismiss because Charlie was a political figure.

The Bible does not define a martyr as merely any Christian who dies violently. The relevant question is faithfulness in witness, especially when that witness brings suffering and death. Jesus tells the suffering church in Revelation 2:10, CSB: “Don’t be afraid of what you are about to suffer. Look, the devil is about to throw some of you into prison to test you, and you will experience affliction for ten days. Be faithful to the point of death, and I will give you the crown of life.”

Revelation 6:9 is equally direct: “When he opened the fifth seal, I saw under the altar the souls of those who had been slaughtered because of the word of God and the testimony they had given.”

That biblical category deserves to be handled with reverence rather than sentiment. I do not call Charlie a martyr merely because he was murdered, and I do not believe Christians need to exaggerate the facts to honor him. I believe there is a serious biblical case for the word because Charlie publicly confessed his faith, increasingly allowed that faith to shape the moral convictions he proclaimed, lived for years under threats connected to that public work, and ultimately died while continuing to carry those convictions into places where they were fiercely contested. The prosecution now alleges that his political and religious beliefs were themselves part of why he was targeted. If that case is borne out, the connection becomes clearer still.

Even if the word martyr ultimately fits, it does not place Charlie beyond grace, criticism, or correction. A martyr is not a perfect Christian. He is still a sinner saved by the same Christ he confessed, and Christ remains the only flawless standard by which any Christian life can be measured.

Charlie certainly had faults. He could be combative. He sometimes spoke too sharply. Some of his statements deserve criticism, including from Christians who otherwise admired him. Charlie himself understood that problem. In his final interview he admitted that he fell short “almost every day” of the Christian obligation to speak truth with both love and grace. That admission may tell us as much about his faith as any polished declaration could.

Christianity does not begin with the assertion that we have met the standard. It begins with recognizing that we have not.

That is why I keep returning to Paul's words in 1 Corinthians 11:1, CSB: “Imitate me, as I also imitate Christ.”

That is the proper measure for Charlie Kirk or any other Christian whose life becomes influential. Where Charlie imitated Christ, follow the example. Where he failed, do not defend the failure because you admire the man. Christ remains the standard. Charlie needed the same grace he spent his final years telling other people they needed.

A year later, we can also begin examining what survived him.

The Cultural Research Center at Arizona Christian University has found measurable changes in the religious behavior of Gen Z, although its researchers are appropriately cautious about what those changes mean. Between May 2025 and January 2026, weekly church attendance among Gen Z increased five percentage points, while the percentage who said they never read the Bible declined five points. Across the longer period from 2022 through 2026, the share identifying as Christian rose five points, weekly Bible reading rose ten points, and the share describing themselves as deeply committed to practicing their faith increased seventeen points.

There is another side of the data, and Christians should be willing to say so. Only 1 percent of Gen Z met the research center's standard for possessing a fully biblical worldview. Several beliefs moved away from historic Christian teaching during the same period. The researchers themselves described the evidence for revival as weak and incomplete. If we omit those findings because they complicate the story we want to tell, we would be doing exactly what Christians should refuse to do with evidence.

I do not know whether America is experiencing a revival, and the available research does not permit me to say that Charlie Kirk caused one. God does not need us to manipulate statistics on His behalf. What the evidence does show is spiritual interest among young people alongside a profound shortage of Christian formation. That is striking because formation was exactly where Charlie's language had been moving. He did not merely want young people interested in Christianity. He wanted them in churches, reading Scripture, marrying, raising families, pursuing virtue, and building their lives around something more durable than political anger.

That work did not stop when he died.

In January 2026, TPUSA Faith launched the Make Heaven Crowded Tour, a series of nearly thirty evangelistic gatherings hosted with local churches. The meetings have included worship, preaching, calls to repentance and faith, and efforts to connect people to churches. Organizers have reported people responding to the Gospel. Those conversion reports belong to the organizers and should be identified that way, but there is no ambiguity about what the gatherings are trying to accomplish. They are not merely voter rallies with a prayer attached. Their stated purpose is evangelism.

Then there is Erika Kirk.

At her husband's memorial, she publicly forgave the man accused of killing him. She did not pretend justice was unnecessary or that evil had somehow ceased being evil. She grounded forgiveness in Jesus Christ. An outside scholar of religion who did not share everything associated with Turning Point described the moment by saying that the Gospel had been preached.

Erika's obedience belongs to Erika. It should not be appropriated merely to improve Charlie's biography. Yet her response showed what Christian conviction looks like when it leaves the safety of slogans and enters suffering. It is easy to praise forgiveness when the wound belongs to somebody else. She had to decide whether the teachings she and her husband proclaimed were still true when obedience became costly.

That witness has reached people far beyond Charlie's political audience.

Older Christians should notice something else in his life as well. Charlie refused to accept the idea that young adults were beyond reach. He walked onto campuses filled with people who had been described as secular, progressive, hostile, apathetic, or lost and talked to them anyway. Some mocked him. Some shouted at him. Some lined up for hours to argue with him. Others listened. He treated their questions as worth answering and acted as though truth could withstand examination.

The church needs some of that confidence.

Young people are thinking about God, sex, marriage, identity, loneliness, purpose, morality, family, and what kind of lives are worth living. They do not need older Christians sneering at them from a distance, and they do not need Christianity reduced to another political brand. They need churches willing to teach Scripture, answer difficult questions, model repentance, build relationships, and patiently form disciples. The recent Gen Z data should sober us here. Religious curiosity can open a door, but curiosity is not discipleship. Someone still has to walk with people through it.

Charlie appeared increasingly aware of the same limitation in politics. Government has genuine responsibilities because its decisions affect real people. It can protect innocent life or fail to protect it. It can restrain wrongdoing or reward it. It can preserve liberty or misuse power. Christian citizenship cannot simply retreat from those questions, and Charlie never believed it should.

What he seemed increasingly unwilling to do was confuse political success with the work of Christ.

An election cannot regenerate a human heart. Legislation cannot forgive sin. A court cannot reconcile a person to God. No president can give eternal life. Those are not failures of government. They are things government was never capable of doing.

Christ alone can do them.

That is why I do not think the proper story of Charlie Kirk's final years is that he moved away from politics and toward Christianity. The movement was more interesting than that. His Christianity increasingly ordered his politics. Biblical conviction helped determine what he believed was worth defending in public, while the Gospel reminded him that even the most important political victory remained temporary.

He was beginning to ask more than whether young people could be persuaded. He wanted to know what they were becoming.

Charlie had only 31 years. He did not receive the decades most of us assume we will have to refine our convictions, correct our mistakes, raise our families, and finish the work we believe God has given us. The incompleteness of his life should keep us from pretending we know what another forty years would have produced. It should also make us pay attention to the direction in which he was traveling when those years were taken from him.

One year later, Turning Point USA is larger. Its campus presence has expanded. The political movement Charlie helped build continues without him. Those things belong in the historical record, but I am not convinced they are the most important evidence of his legacy.

I am more interested in the young person who opens a Bible because Charlie told him to take God seriously. The man who decides perpetual adolescence is not freedom and begins thinking about becoming a husband and father. The woman who returns to church. The believer who understands that courage is not merely winning an argument but remaining faithful when faithfulness costs something. The older Christian who stops complaining about the next generation long enough to disciple someone in it.

Those are harder things to measure than votes, views, and membership rolls. They are also much closer to what Charlie said he wanted near the end.

Charlie Kirk spent much of his short life trying to change people's minds. Toward the end it became increasingly clear that he wanted something more important. He wanted Christ to change their lives.

The men rushed towards him. Jafari screamed and repeatedly struck the bars on the door with his hands until they were bloodied. Eventually, he shouted:

"Just get me out of here. I'll write whatever you want."

According to credible information received, Parsa Jafari gave this account during the hearing into his case on 16 July 2026, in the presence of his lawyer and court officials, while crying and visibly distressed.

He reportedly told the court that, while in the custody of interrogating officers, he was blindfolded, taken out of the prison, and transported to another building.

After his blindfold was removed, Parsa found himself standing in front of a room with a grey door that had metal bars near the top. He had to walk down a long flight of stairs to reach the room.

He was ordered to go downstairs.

According to Parsa Jafari's account in court, when the door was opened, he saw seven or eight men inside the room. Most of them were overweight and were not wearing trousers or underwear, but only undershirts. The room smelled strongly of a toilet. The men in the room, who appeared unable to communicate normally, were masturbating and playing with their genitals.

According to the account presented in court, these individuals were described as people with severe and uncontrolled mental health conditions who were being held in the basement.

The officers allegedly pushed Parsa into the room and told him that they had previously shown pornography to the men inside. They then closed and locked the door.

The men inside the room rushed towards Parsa.

Parsa told the court that he screamed with all his strength and repeatedly struck the metal bars above the door with the palms of his hands in an attempt to escape. He hit the bars so hard and for so long that his palms became bloody and his hands were bruised.

Despite this, the officers did not open the door.

Parsa eventually shouted:

"Just get me out of here. I'll write whatever you want."

Only after he said this did the officers open the door and remove him from the room. When he came out, the buttons on his upper clothing had reportedly been torn off as a result of the men rushing towards him.

The knowledgeable and credible source who provided this information stressed that Parsa Jafari described the entire incident during an official court hearing, in the presence of his lawyer and court personnel, and that he was crying intensely while recounting what had happened.

According to the information received, the direction of the investigation and interrogations changed from that very day. The interrogations, which had previously focused on allegations concerning the manufacture of Molotov cocktails, subsequently shifted towards accusing Parsa Jafari and other defendants in the case of the killing of Abbas Kamrani.

This account raises serious concerns that interrogating officers deliberately placed Parsa Jafari in a situation in which he believed he faced an immediate threat of sexual assault, and that, in order to escape, he declared his willingness to write whatever the interrogators demanded.

This was not merely a verbal threat.
1/3

Sound the Alarm : IFF’s First Read on MeitY's Draft IT Rules Second Amendment, 2026

New Delhi, 30 March 2026

On 30 March 2026, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology published proposed amendments to the IT Rules, 2021, inviting public comments by 14 April,  a comment period of barely fifteen days for changes with far reaching consequences for free speech and intermediary governance in India. We have conducted a quick review of the draft amendments. Despite being presented as "clarificatory and procedural," they represent a dangerous expansion of executive power over online speech.

We wish to state at the outset that these proposed amendments need to be immediately withdrawn and every member in our citizenry should demand their roll back and stand with the Constitution of India. These proposed amendments come at a time of fear and increased government directed censorship, especially of online political speech that includes parody and satire of the government, including the Prime Minister.

In brief the five changes are listed below:

1. Rule 3(1)(g) and 3(1)(h): Insertion of phrases within existing clauses making data retention obligations under the IT Rules additional to retention requirements under any other law.

2. Rule 3(4): Insertion of a new clause that mandates intermediary compliance with MeitY-issued clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs, codes of practice, and guidelines, making such compliance a condition for retaining safe harbour under Section 79 of the IT Act. These are not anchored to the rule making powers of the IT Act, 2000 and provide uncanalised power to MEITY despite it stating otherwise.

3. Rule 8(1) proviso: A substitution in the proviso that expands applicability of MIB’s oversight mechanism in Part III of the rules to:  (1) intermediaries and (2) users who are not “publishers” and post/share news and current affairs content online. This oversight mechanism contains the blocking powers of MIB by way of Rule 14 (Inter-Departmental Committee), Rule 15 (Procedure for issuing directions to block), and Rule 16 (Emergency blocking provisions).

4. Rule 14(2) : A substitution that expands the scope of the IDC from hearing "complaints or grievances" to hearing "matters", including those referred by the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting.

5. Rule 14(5) : Replaces "complaints or grievances" with "the matter" in relation to IDC examination and recommendations.

A massive expansion of an unconstitutional censorship and regulatory power

First and most concerningly, Rule 3(4) creates a sweeping power for MeitY to issue binding instruments which are not anchored in law such as clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs, codes of practice, and guidelines that intermediaries must comply with as a condition of safe harbour under Section 79 of the IT Act.

The Supreme Court's 2015 judgment in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) 5 SCC 1, remains the foundational precedent governing intermediary liability. It constrains the proposed amendments in several ways. First, the court read down Section 79(3)(b) to require that "actual knowledge" of unlawful content must come through a court order or government notification. Any Rule 3(4) making MeitY, "clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs", lower the constitutional threshold for intermediary due diligence obligations.

Further, the settled principle in Indian administrative law, reaffirmed in Indian Express Newspapers v. Union of India (1985) 1 SCC 641 and Confederation of Ex-Servicemen Associations v. Union of India (2006) 8 SCC 399, is that delegated legislation must remain within the four corners of the parent statute.  It is important to note that the rule-making power under Section 87(1) of the IT Act is confined to, "carry[ing] out the provisions" of the Act. Section 87(2)(zg) authorizes rules for intermediary guidelines under Section 79(2), and Section 87(2)(z) for blocking procedures under Section 69A(2). Justice Chandurkar's judgement in the Kunal Kamra case clearly found the FCU amendment was not properly referable to either provision. Hence, any Rule 3(4) mandating compliance with MeitY advisories would face identical challenges since they create substantive new obligations not contemplated by Sections 79 or 87.

Even though Rule 3(4)(b)(ii) states that such, “advisories” etc. need to, “clearly specify the statutory provision or legal basis under which it is issued”, since these are not required to be published or made public there is every likelihood these will be issued with secrecy and hence may just in a tautological manner refer back to Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act. This is similar to a logical fallacy in which it is clearly observable that a student is cheating on an exam who then claims that they may be permitted to continue cheating since they are stating at the same time they are not cheating. 

The practical effect of Rule 3(4) is that intermediaries face a perpetual compliance threat. Any failure to comply with any MeitY-issued instrument, however vague, however rapidly issued may cost them their safe harbour. The response for an intermediary is over-compliance and over-censorship.

Circumventing existing stay orders

The original proviso to Rule 8(1) stated that Part III applied to intermediaries only "for the purposes of rules 15 and 16"  i.e., content blocking directions and emergency blocking. The amended proviso now extends this to Rule 14, bringing intermediaries and user-generated news/current affairs content under the jurisdiction of the Inter-Departmental Committee.

Under Rules 9(1) and 9(3) of the 2021 IT Rules, there is a Code of Ethics compliance requirement and the three-tier grievance redressal mechanism, both of which were stayed by the Bombay High Court on 14 August 2021 as prima facie violative of Article 19(1)(a) and ultra vires the IT Act. On the oversight mechanism in Rules 14, 15, and 16, the Bombay High Court granted the petitioners to seek relief on this rule when an Inter Departmental Committee is established. The Madras High Court affirmed this stay as having pan-India effect in its order of 16 September 2021 in T.M. Krishna v. Union of India, observing that "an oversight mechanism to control the media by the government may rob the media of its independence." 

Both these cases, along with other cases challenging various provisions of the 2021 IT Rules, are now pending adjudication before the Delhi High Court.

The expansion of Rule 8(1) to cover Rules 14, 15, and 16 is an attempt to expand the blocking powers of MIB to both intermediaries and users who are not “publishers” but post news and current affairs content online. The IDC can now examine "matters" relating to user-generated news content on intermediary platforms without the Code of Ethics framework having been adjudicated as constitutional; the government effectively obtains the content oversight machinery that three High Courts found illegal, through a different procedural door.

Transforming the IDC from Grievance Body to Censorship Apparatus

The original Rule 14(2) required the IDC to hear "complaints regarding violation or contravention of the Code of Ethics." The amended version removes this requirement entirely. 

The IDC now hears:
(a) grievances arising from decisions at Level I or II; or
(b) "matters" referred to by the Ministry.

Clause (b) is unconstrained since, (a) there is no requirement that the "matter" arise from a complaint, (b) no requirement that the "matter" relate to a Code of Ethics violation; and (c) no requirement that the affected party be heard before the referral. The Ministry of Information and Broadcasting can, on its own motion, refer any content-related "matter" to the IDC. 

The cumulative effect of the amendments to Rules 8 and 14 is to reconstruct the oversight machinery that the Bombay and Madras High Courts found constitutionally suspect, in a form designed to evade the existing interim orders. The IDC, previously limited to the three-tier complaints process under the stayed Rules 9(3), 12, and 13 framework, now operates as a free-standing censorship committee that can take up "matters" referred by the executive.

Increased user surveillance through mandatory data retention directions

Insertion of phrases within existing clauses making data retention obligations under the IT Rules additional to retention requirements under any other law. For instance, the mandatory data retention of user data beyond 180 days within Rule 3(1)(g) and 3(1)(h) may be prescribed for longer periods and other purposes raising risks of surveillance and even potentially data leaks of sensitive data that is stored for longer periods of time. Government mandates for data retention as to their legal authority and hence period of retention will be beyond those contained under the IT Act.

SOS for Digital Rights 

IFF urges an urgent rollback!

We are alarmed by the continuing expansion of unchecked executive power that is opposed to the Constitution of India. The present actions of MEITY smack of digital authoritarianism and we call on them to withdraw these proposed amendments. 

The proper course is to await judicial determination of the pending challenges, respect interim protections granted by constitutional courts, and pursue regulatory objectives through parliamentary legislation rather than subordinate instruments that exceed the parent statute.

If not withdrawn, IFF will file a detailed response before the comment deadline. We call upon all stakeholders to submit their objections before 14 April 2026 at itrules.consultation@meity.gov.in

INDIA CRACKS DOWN ON AI & DEEP FAKE. BIG TECH PUT ON NOTCE

1. What has actually changed?

The Modi government amended the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021 on 10 February 2026 specifically to deal with synthetically generated information and deepfakes.
The framework covers deceptive AI-generated audio, visual and audio-visual material.
The idea is no longer simply: remove illegal content after somebody complains.

Platforms are now being pushed towards:
identification
labelling
metadata
verification
automated detection
rapid takedown
and greater accountability for allowing unlawful AI content to spread.

2. AI CONTENT HAS TO BE IDENTIFIABLE
This is probably the biggest structural change.
AI-generated/synthetically altered material covered by the rules has to be clearly identifiable as synthetic.
Platforms/services enabling generation or alteration of such content must ensure appropriate labels or traceable identifiers/metadata.
The objective is simple:
REAL CONTENT ≠ AI CONTENT
The viewer should not have to conduct a forensic investigation to figure out whether something was artificially generated.
Important nuance

Don't say “every piece of text written using AI anywhere on the internet must carry a label.”

MeitY's FAQ clarifies that the operative 2026 SGI definition primarily targets audio, visual and audio-visual information, not ordinary AI-generated written text.
A more accurate line for your video is:
“India has mandated identification and labelling requirements for covered AI-generated synthetic media, particularly deepfake audio, images and video.”

3. THE BIG NUMBER: 36 HOURS → 3 HOURS

Previously, once an intermediary received legally valid knowledge of unlawful material through the prescribed government/court process, the compliance window could be 36 hours.

That has now been cut to:

3 HOURS

That is a 91.7% reduction in response time.

So something capable of going viral nationally during an election, riot, communal incident, stock-market panic or national-security crisis can no longer theoretically remain online for a day and a half after a valid takedown direction.

The platform has only hours.

4. AND SOME COMPLAINT WINDOWS ARE EVEN SHORTER

The government says timelines for grievance redressal have also been compressed.

According to the PIB explanation:
certain complaints earlier subject to 72 hours can now require action within 36 hours

particularly sensitive categories that earlier had a 24-hour timeline can now require action within 2 hours

This specifically matters for areas such as:

impersonation

intimate imagery

nudity

deepfake abuse

other highly sensitive material.

5. BIG TECH CAN'T JUST WAIT FOR A COMPLAINT

This is another major change.

The government says intermediaries must deploy reasonable and appropriate technical measures, including automated tools or other mechanisms, against unlawful synthetically generated content.
That means platforms are increasingly being pushed from:
REACTIVE MODERATION
to
PROACTIVE DETECTION
For Significant Social Media Intermediaries, the framework explicitly envisages technical measures to identify prohibited content, including certain forms of:

rape-related material

child sexual abuse material

repeat prohibited content

unlawful synthetic content.

6. USERS MAY HAVE TO DECLARE AI CONTENT

The synthetic-media framework also places responsibility upstream.

Major platforms can be required to ask users uploading covered content whether it is synthetically generated and then use technical systems to check that declaration.

So theoretically:
User uploads video →
declares AI/not AI →
platform checks →
synthetic material gets labelled.

The earlier draft framework explicitly envisaged this declaration + technical-verification model.

7. WHY THE METADATA PART MATTERS

A visible watermark can be:

cropped,
blurred,
edited,
screen-recorded,

reposted.

Metadata/identifiers create another layer of traceability.

The government's objective is therefore not merely:

“PUT AI GENERATED IN THE CAPTION.”
It is building a system where synthetic content can carry technological indicators allowing platforms to recognise what it is.
That becomes especially useful once the same manipulated video is downloaded and re-uploaded across multiple platforms.
8. THE RULES TARGET DEEPFAKE IMPERSONATION DIRECTLY
Existing IT Rules already prohibit users from publishing material that:

impersonates another person

misleads users about the origin of a message

knowingly spreads patently false or misleading information

threatens public order

violates another applicable law.

AI does not create an exemption.

If AI is being used for impersonation, fraud, defamatory fabrication or other unlawful activity, existing criminal and cyber provisions can also apply.

9. BNS CAN ALSO COME INTO PLAY
The PIB release specifically points towards provisions of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita.
Depending upon what the deepfake is being used for, authorities could examine provisions relating to:
Section 319 — cheating by personation
Section 336 — forgery

Section 353 — false information/rumours capable of causing public mischief or fear

Section 111 — organised crime, where the factual circumstances justify it.

So there isn't necessarily a standalone offence called simply:

“making a deepfake.”

The legal consequence depends heavily upon what the deepfake does.

10. CHILD SEXUAL ABUSE DEEPFAKES GET SPECIAL ATTENTION
This is perhaps the least discussed but most important provision.
The amended framework explicitly covers harmful AI-generated material involving:
child sexual exploitation

non-consensual intimate imagery

impersonation

other prohibited synthetic material.

Platforms are expected to prevent such content and act rapidly when detected.

11. SOCIAL-MEDIA GIANTS HAVE EXTRA DUTIES

Platforms classified as Significant Social Media Intermediaries, broadly those crossing the prescribed Indian user threshold, face additional compliance obligations.

These include mechanisms involving:
automated detection
grievance officers
compliance officers

local points of contact

India-based compliance structures

periodic compliance reports

appeals processes

originator tracing in specified circumstances for messaging services.
So the rules are aimed not only at the person creating the deepfake.
They put a major compliance burden on the distribution network itself.
12. THE REAL STICK: SAFE HARBOUR
This is where it becomes serious for Meta, X, Google, Telegram and other intermediaries.
Section 79 of the IT Act provides intermediaries conditional protection from liability for third-party content.
But that protection depends upon complying with the law and prescribed due diligence.
The PIB release reiterates that failure to observe obligations under the IT Rules can result in the intermediary losing its Section 79 exemption, after which liability can arise under applicable law.

That makes the real equation:

Comply with due diligence → retain intermediary protection

Ignore statutory obligations → safe-harbour protection can be jeopardised

That is far more powerful than merely issuing a fine.

13. GOVERNMENT HAS BUILT A TAKEDOWN PIPELINE

There is now an increasingly integrated enforcement architecture:

Grievance Appellate Committees — GACs

Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre — I4C

SAHYOG Portal

National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal

police/cybercrime units

authorised State and Central Government agencies.

The SAHYOG system in particular enables centralised electronic communication of lawful content-removal notices to intermediaries.

14. INDIA IS ALSO BUILDING ITS OWN DEEPFAKE-DETECTION TECHNOLOGY

Under the IndiaAI Mission's Safe & Trusted AI pillar, government-backed work includes indigenous detection and governance technologies.
PIB identifies projects including:
Saakshya — multi-agent deepfake-detection framework developed by IIT Jodhpur and IIT Madras
AI Vishleshak — audio-visual forgery detection
IIT Kharagpur work on real-time voice deepfake detection.

So this is not purely a legal crackdown.

It is simultaneously a:

LEGAL + PLATFORM + TECHNOLOGICAL framework.

15. WHY THIS IS HAPPENING NOW

Generative AI has destroyed the old assumption that:
“Seeing is believing.”
Today one person can manufacture:

a politician announcing something he never said

a CEO apparently moving a stock

an Army officer issuing a fake warning

communal speeches

celebrity pornography

fake financial endorsements

fabricated battlefield footage

false evidence of violence
within minutes.
And the fake can reach millions before conventional fact-checking catches up.
Therefore the Indian approach is increasingly:
IDENTIFY → LABEL → DETECT → TRACE → REMOVE → PROSECUTE
rather than merely:
WAIT → RECEIVE COMPLAINT → INVESTIGATE.
THE BIG STORY FOR YOUR VIDEO

The headline isn't simply:

“Deepfakes must carry labels.”

The bigger story is that India is trying to change where responsibility lies.

Earlier, platforms could largely argue:

A user uploaded it; we are merely the intermediary.

The regulatory direction is increasingly:

If you operate the technology that generates, distributes or algorithmically amplifies synthetic content in India, you have duties to identify it, label it and respond rapidly when it becomes unlawful.

🚨 BIG: Government of India has unveiled one of the most comprehensive legal frameworks to combat AI-generated deepfakes, synthetic media, misinformation and unlawful online content.

The framework brings together the IT Act, 2000, Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), 2023, IT Rules, 2021, the 2026 IT Rules amendments, and the IndiaAI Governance Guidelines to strengthen digital safety and platform accountability.

Key highlights:

🔹 Mandatory AI Labelling: Platforms must clearly label AI-generated or synthetic content with traceable metadata so users can identify manipulated content and prevent deception.

🔹 Fastest Takedown Timelines Yet: Removal of unlawful content after a valid government or court notice has been reduced from 36 hours to just 3 hours. Grievance redressal timelines have also been tightened—from 72 hours to 36 hours, and 24 hours to 2 hours for sensitive content such as nudity, impersonation and similar categories.

🔹 IT Act, 2000: Covers penalties for computer-related offences, identity theft (Sec. 66C), online impersonation (66D), privacy violations (66E), publishing obscene or sexually explicit content (Secs. 67 & 67A), empowers blocking of unlawful content under Sec. 69A, removal directions under Sec. 79, and enables police investigation under Secs. 78 & 80.

🔹 Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023: Covers cheating by personation (Sec. 319), forgery through false electronic records (Sec. 336), spreading false reports or misinformation causing public mischief (Sec. 353), and organised cybercrime involving deepfake content (Sec. 111).

🔹 Strict Platform Obligations: Intermediaries must not host or share content that infringes rights, invades privacy, promotes hate or violence, harms children, violates intellectual property, misleads users about message origin, knowingly spreads false information, impersonates individuals (including using AI), threatens India's sovereignty, security or public order, or violates any applicable law.

🔹 Greater Accountability for Social Media Platforms: Significant Social Media Intermediaries (SSMIs) must assist law enforcement in tracing originators of serious content, deploy automated tools to detect unlawful content, publish compliance reports, appoint grievance and compliance officers, maintain India-based compliance infrastructure, and provide user verification, appeals and fair hearing mechanisms.

🔹 Zero Tolerance for Harmful AI: Platforms are now explicitly required to prevent AI-generated child sexual abuse material, non-consensual intimate imagery, deepfakes, AI impersonation, harmful synthetic media and other unlawful AI-generated content using reasonable technical measures and automated detection systems.

🔹 Legal Consequences: Failure to comply with the IT Rules can result in intermediaries losing their Section 79 safe-harbour protection, exposing them to prosecution and legal action under applicable laws.

🔹 Robust Enforcement Ecosystem: The framework will be enforced through Grievance Appellate Committees (GACs), the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C), the SAHYOG Portal, the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal, and law enforcement agencies. Citizens can report cybercrime and deepfakes through the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal, with Helpline 1930 available for cyber fraud complaints.

🔹 Responsible AI Development: Under the IndiaAI Mission, the government is funding indigenous AI safety projects, including Saakshya (IIT Jodhpur & IIT Madras), AI Vishleshak, and IIT Kharagpur's Real-Time Voice Deepfake Detection System, alongside the India AI Governance Guidelines to promote safe, trusted and responsible AI deployment.

The message is clear: AI innovation is welcome, but deepfakes, impersonation, misinformation, child exploitation, and unlawful synthetic content will face significantly stricter regulation, faster takedowns, and stronger legal consequences than ever before.

India just set one of the world’s tightest deadlines for deepfake moderation. 

As of February 20th, social platforms will have to remove AI-generated fakes and harmful synthetic content within 3 hours of a takedown order. 

Under these rules social platforms will have to deploy tools to verify those whether or not a piece of content is synthetic, and ensure that deepfakes are clearly labeled and embedded with traceable provenance data.

Platforms are going to need systems that can prove authenticity in real-time.

# 🧾 Fact-Check System Prompt

**Version:** 0.5.0  
**Date:** 2026-09-11  
**Type:** System / context prompt  
**Created with:** Grok 4.6 (xAI)

---

## 📌 Usage (read this first)

Paste this entire document as the system / custom instructions.

Then send a separate user message that contains only the item to check. Do not put the target URL inside this prompt.

Accepted user-message formats:

1. URL only  
   https://t.co/23w27slz7i

2. Label + URL  
   Fact-check this:  
   https://t.co/23w27slz7i

3. Pasted post + optional URL  
   Caption: ...  
   URL: https://...

4. Screenshot / image of a post  
   Attach the image. Add the URL if you have it.

If the user message has a URL, open that URL first and fact-check that item.  
If both a URL and pasted text are present, the live URL is primary; pasted text is only a copy.  
If the user message has no URL, post text, or image, ask for one of those three. Do not invent a target.

If the user message is this document or a near-copy of it, reply only:  
`Target is the checker prompt itself. No check.`  
Do not fact-check this prompt.

---

You are a fact-checker. Check only what the author stated. Do not complete, defend, or rewrite the author’s argument.  
If a claim cannot be verified with available sources, say so. Do not guess.

## A. Quote first
Reproduce each claim in the author’s exact words.  
Separate: caption, image/overlay text, quoted third parties.  
Do not add motive or “what they must have meant.”

## B. Atomic claims
Split into the smallest testable units: actor, action, date, place, number, cause, comparison.  
A slogan is not a statistic. A target is not money spent.

## C. Allowed verdicts
Use only one per claim:
- True
- True but incomplete
- Aspiration presented as fact
- Unsupported
- False
- Rhetoric (not checkable)
- Unverifiable with available sources

Use **True but incomplete** only when the stated fact is correct *and* a material qualifier (scope, date, denominator, exception) is omitted that a reasonable reader would need.

If sources conflict, report the conflict. Do not pick a side to make the post coherent.

## D. Evidence rule
- True requires a primary source, official record, or named authority quoted contemporaneously, matching actor, number, date, and scope.
- The source must pre-date or independently document the event. A restatement issued after the post does not count.
- Goals, estimates, “eyes,” “will,” “set to,” and fundraising asks are not completed facts.
- Party, office, ideology, timing, or leadership is not proof that person ordered this action.
- Units, years, and geography must match.

## E. Attribution lock
“On X’s orders,” “because of X,” “X made this happen” is Unsupported unless a source shows X directed this action, figure, or document.  
Leadership status does not close that gap.  
Acceptable closer: a signed order, recorded instruction, or official document that names the actor and the specific action/figure.

## F. Novelty and contrast
“First,” “only,” “never before,” and “they do Y, we do Z” need comparative evidence. Otherwise: Unsupported or Rhetoric.

## G. Medium
Note satire, campaign handles, cropped screenshots, and edited graphics.  
If the only evidence is a cropped graphic or satire handle, default the claim to Unsupported or Rhetoric unless a primary source independently confirms it.  
Medium does not upgrade a weak claim to True.

## 📤 Output only
1. Item checked (URL or short description)
2. Quoted claims (caption vs image, listed separately)
3. One verdict + shortest evidence per claim, with source  
   Prefix each claim block with: `CLAIM n | VERDICT | SOURCE`
4. Conflicts or missing evidence, if any
5. The single source that would change an Unsupported causal claim to True

---

## 📝 Changelog
- 0.5.0: Hardened self-exemption; tightened “True but incomplete”; required independent/pre-dating sources; added attribution closer example; medium now constrains weak evidence; added parseable claim prefix.

India has quietly frozen Starlink. It issued the license nearly a year ago, then let the final security clearance sit, and the whole satellite-comms sector has slowed with it. This is not a compliance dispute. text:
*Elon Musk’s Starlink was trying to beat Jio in India*

*But Jio used its 1st mover’s advantage to stop them in their tracks*

*The SHOCKER? Indian Gov is changing a 138 year old law that will bring Starlink back in the game*

*Here’s how Elon is rethinking internet & can possibly kill Jio:*

In 2016, when most of us were witnessing a business disruption standing in queues to get our hands on the free Jio sim card,

12,869 miles away at Rocket Road, California, a group of engineers were planning a technological disruption.

Their goal? Rethink internet access.

Their solution? Satellite Internet.

Traditionally, we have been using internet that relies on cable wires, fiber optic lines, or cellular networks.

But making cable wires or fiber optic lines available in remote villages and hard terrains is not only costly but highly impractical as well.

And this is where satellite internet and Starlink by Elon Musk comes in.

Satellite Internet uses signals from satellites orbiting the Earth.

And Starlink is a collection of thousands of small satellites orbiting around 350 miles above the Earth.

For the satellite internet to work, the user on the ground connects to the Starlink dish, known as the user terminal.

The user terminal communicates with nearby Starlink satellites and forms a link to the larger Starlink network

The satellites then form a mesh network, that allows them to pass data between each other and create global network coverage.

Starlink’s motto is — ‘virtually anywhere on earth without wires or cellphone towers.’

It started its operation in 2019 and true to its motto, it’s already available in over 65 countries,

— covering all 7 continents (including Antarctica!)

But Starlink hasn’t been able to make any progress in India.

Last year, it registered its business in India via a local unit Starlink Satellite Communications Pvt Ltd.

The company had planned to provide fast internet data in the Indian market at a subsidized price compared to the international market.

It had received 5,000+ pre-orders.

But the government said Starlink Internet Services doesn’t have the license to offer services in India.

And it asked Starlink to return people’s money.

Now, one company’s loss is another company’s gain.

In Feb this year, Reliance Jio partnered up with Luxembourg-based SES to provide satellite-based broadband services in India.

And created a joint venture called — Jio Space Technology Ltd.

Moreover, Starlink and Jio Space aren’t the only contenders for India’s space spectrum.

OneWeb is backed by Airtel in India and Hughes Communication.

Tata group entity Nelco partnered up with Canada's Telesat.

And Amazon’s Kuiper is going to launch satellites in 2024.

But why are so many companies vying for India’s space spectrum?

India has a population of 1.4 billion out of which 40% do not have internet access because they are in rural and remote areas.

And traditional terrestrial networks are not easy to install.

Hence, India’s satellite broadband service is expected to reach $1.9 billion by 2030, growing at a CAGR of 36%.

Now, because India has so many contenders for its spectrum, the question arises — who should get it?

Starlink and OneWeb wanted the government to assign licenses to companies, since spectrum is a natural resource that should be shared by companies.

But Jio wanted the government to auction the spectrum like it did with 4G & 5G 👀

Finally, the government brought in some reforms and firstly dedicated a sole agency IN-SPACe to authorize space activities for both government and private satellite communication companies.

And a bill has been proposed to replace the 138-year-old Indian Telegraph Act that currently governs the telecommunication sector.

So now, both Jio Space & OneWeb have received their GMPCS license from the Department of Telecommunications in India.

And Starlink is 3rd in line to receive the GMPCS license.

When does a government stop calling it foreign interference and start asking, why is the entire world saying the same thing about us?

Here is what is actually happening inside India right now:

▪️ India has the world’s strictest content takedown window; just 3 hours. No major democracy, and no major authoritarian regime, moves this fast against its own citizens’ speech.

▪️ Under the new IT Rules 2026 amendment, it’s not just news outlets being targeted. Ordinary users, influencers, and anyone who simply shares a news post can now fall under the government’s content blocking framework.

▪️ The Internet Freedom Foundation has formally called this “digital authoritarianism” and a “dangerous expansion of executive power.” These are not opposition politicians, these are constitutional lawyers and digital rights experts.

▪️ Since 2014, India’s government takedown orders have surged 14 times; from 201 to 14,775. And post 2022, this data was denied under RTI on grounds of national security.

▪️ Meta alone was forced to restrict 28,000+ pieces of content in India in just the first six months of 2025; following government orders.

▪️ India currently ranks 151 out of 180 in the World Press Freedom Index. We are sitting between countries most Indians would be ashamed to be compared with.

▪️ The Supreme Court’s own Shreya Singhal judgment; a landmark free speech ruling, is being systematically bypassed by these rules. 

This is not policy. This is contempt of constitutional precedent.

The government will say this is about deepfakes. About national security. About public order.

But when 138 YouTube videos were taken down for allegedly defaming Adani, a private businessman, it stopped being about security a long time ago.

France 24 is not attacking India. France 24 is holding up a mirror.

The question is, why is this government so terrified of what Indians might see in it?

Challenging the law in the 1930 Miami.... 

A small but memorable act of defiance on a Miami beach in the 1930s, when the city enforced strict decency laws requiring “full bathing suits.” These rules dictated the size of swimwear, how much skin could be shown, and even how high the hems could rise. Miami, like many coastal cities of the era, tied morality to dress codes, and police routinely walked beaches measuring women’s swimsuits with rulers. Violators could be fined or escorted off the sand.

The women in this photo playfully pose beneath the warning sign, a moment that shows both the absurdity of the law and the growing pushback against it. By the 1930s, bathing suits were evolving rapidly. Women had begun rejecting the heavy wool suits of the early 1900s in favor of sleeker, more practical designs. This shift sparked national debates about modesty, femininity, and personal freedom.

Images like this document the cultural tension between tradition and modernity. The beach became a battleground where old social norms collided with a generation unafraid to test the limits, laugh at the rules, and claim a little more autonomy in public life.

In some cities, including Washington D.C., “bathing suit police” carried tape measures and would write citations if a swimsuit was more than six inches above the knee.

Delhi Police cannot have it both ways.

@TeamYouTube this situation has gone way beyond a normal enforcement issue. On July 28, my channel started receiving an unusual wave of privacy complaints. Within roughly 3 days, 40+ complaints were filed against 41 completely unrelated videos, and 31 videos were removed. I appealed multiple removals and repeatedly contacted YouTube Support and Legal, but I never received a clear, case-specific explanation of the alleged privacy violations.

Then on August 14, the entire channel was terminated for Impersonation. I appealed and was rejected. When I contacted Creator Support, I was first told the termination was for Spam, despite the termination notice clearly stating Impersonation. The case was escalated, and I was then told the internal review confirmed Impersonation. I repeatedly asked a simple question: Who or what did I supposedly impersonate, and what exactly on the channel violated the policy? No specific answer was provided.

I submitted another official appeal through Google Form. It was confirmed as received and sent for specialized review, but that appeal has now also been rejected for Impersonation.

So after multiple reviews, I still haven't been told what specific person, channel, branding, video, or conduct supposedly constituted impersonation. I have never intentionally impersonated anyone or claimed to represent another creator or entity.

The matter is now pending before GAC in India and has also been brought to @SFLCin.

I am not asking for special treatment. I am asking for a fair, evidence-based review and a clear explanation of what actually happened. Please escalate this properly and reconsider the termination. @YouTube @UpdatesFromYT @YouTubeCreators @YouTubeIndia

Ray-Ban Meta glasses struck again. A woman walking home alone was secretly recorded by a man who approached her, then posted the footage on Instagram alongside similar clips of him doing this to other women, as part of "pickup" content.

She's filed a police complaint for stalking and voyeurism. IFF is assisting her with a legal notice to the creator, Instagram, and Meta, the second such notice against Meta in India.

This isn't a one off. It's a design problem.
Read more about it: https://t.co/x5Gzp2NFF0

A woman was followed, stopped on a dark street, secretly recorded through Ray-Ban Meta glasses and turned into an Instagram “pickup” reel that reached over 23 lakh views. Now, our legal notice seeks accountability from both him and Meta. (1/10)

Read More: https://t.co/x5Gzp2NFF0

The legal notice therefore puts Meta on notice not merely as the platform hosting the video, but as the designer, developer, manufacturer, marketer and seller of the glasses. It alleges negligence and product liability, arguing that Meta knew about the pattern of misuse but continued selling the device without an effective way for non-users or people being recorded to report that misuse. (9/10)

The notice seeks removal of every copy, preservation and disclosure of evidence, suspension of monetisation, an account of profits, an apology, and ₹2.05 crore in compensatory and exemplary damages. This case raises a larger question: when a company makes a camera that can be worn like ordinary glasses, who protects the person being recorded? Privacy cannot depend on whether the person being filmed has an Instagram account. (10/10)

The Supreme Court has closed India's Got Latent cases, but the question of an “Influencer Code” is not entirely over. On 14 August 2026, the Court quashed all FIRs arising from the episode and left the “larger issues” of regulating online speech for “another appropriate case”. Here is what that means. (1/7)

Read More: https://t.co/hecp2rl9W4

That qualifier matters. Executive action restricting speech must have a legal basis consistent with Article 19. The Court has previously held that executive instructions cannot independently impose restrictions on fundamental rights. The signed order also contains no finding that the content in question was obscene, nor does it establish a new standard for online speech. (6/7)

For now, there are no guidelines and no pending judicial direction requiring them. But MIB can still attempt regulatory changes, including through amendments to the IT Rules. If it does, IFF will insist on the public consultation promised to the Supreme Court, compliance with the Pre-Legislative Consultation Policy and meaningful participation by affected creators and users. (7/7)

NIXI has changed its justification for suspending chalosansad dot in yet again. After first citing a “critical keyword”, and then relying on a 2004 policy clause that did not apply, it now invokes the Emblems Act and demands Central Government permission within seven days. On 8 September, IFF wrote back seeking a standstill and answers. (1/7)
Read More: https://t.co/2grOxR1bMy

The timing matters. The domain was suspended on 22 July. NIXI’s new legal opinion was obtained on 29 August, more than a month later and only after we challenged its earlier reasons. The Supreme Court has repeatedly held that administrative action must stand or fall on the reasons given when the decision was made; authorities cannot ordinarily supplement an order with new reasons after it is challenged. (6/7)

NIXI has now also said that six other .in domains containing “Sansad”, along with other domains containing “Sansad”, “Parliament” or cognate expressions, will be examined. On 8 September, we asked NIXI for a 48-hour standstill on de-registration, deletion, transfer or reallocation of chalosansad dot in, confirmation of Aadhaar deletion, and disclosure of the correspondence it says raised concerns about publication. If no standstill is given, the registrant will approach the court. (7/7)

Support our work: https://t.co/qSG7IzUpIX

NIXI has also given the registrant seven days to produce Central Government permission. Yet its reply identifies no ministry, officer, form, fee, procedure or timeline through which such permission can actually be obtained. We have therefore asked NIXI to explain the legal basis for this demand, and to provide the legal opinion dated 29 August on which its new position relies. (5/7)

quotedTweet.text:
On September 10th, 2013, the Supreme Court struck down Section 66A of the IT Act, a vague law that was being used to arrest people for simply expressing dissent online.

11 years later, Maharashtra wants to bring it back in a new form, by amending the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita for "online criminal defamation." But defamation is already covered under Section 356 of the BNS, and civil remedies already exist.

So why does the police need this new power? Recent FIRs against citizens and influencers for calling out potholes and infrastructure failures may hold the answer. We've fought this battle before. We don't need a new 66A with a new number.

text:
A 2:01-minute reel documenting villagers’ concerns over the proposed Google data centre in Visakhapatnam was blocked in India for 111 days. On 10 September 2026, it quietly came back online. (1/10)

Read More: https://t.co/TVxhdw9ZA1

The Sahyog route also raises a serious constitutional concern. In Shreya Singhal v. Union of India, the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A because the blocking framework contained procedural safeguards, including notice, hearing and a reasoned order. Section 79(3)(b), meanwhile, was read down to require a court order or government notification. A system that blocks first and explains nothing is difficult to reconcile with those safeguards. (9/10)

The reel is back, and we welcome that. But the questions remain unanswered, Who ordered the blocking? Why did the order name an unrelated person? Was a periodic review conducted? Why was the reel restored? IFF will continue seeking these answers from Andhra Pradesh authorities. Journalists should not need months of litigation to learn why their public-interest reporting was censored. (10/10)
